params.question: Which combination of interventions converts unmodified ECT into the modified form used today?

answers.text: Bilateral electrode placement, EEG monitoring, and written informed consent

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These are important parts of the ECT procedure, but they are not the defining modifications. EEG monitoring and consent are standard practice elements, not what distinguishes modified from unmodified ECT.

answers.text: Short-acting general anaesthesia, succinylcholine (muscle relaxant), and oxygenation/ventilation support

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. These three interventions eliminate the violent muscle contractions that caused fractures and dislocations in unmodified ECT, while preserving the therapeutic cerebral seizure.

answers.text: Higher electrical stimulus intensity, longer seizure duration, and post-ictal monitoring

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Modified ECT uses carefully titrated stimulus doses, not higher intensity. The modification refers to patient-safety measures (anaesthesia, muscle relaxation, ventilation), not changes to the electrical stimulus.

answers.text: Propranolol for heart rate control, diazepam for sedation, and continuous blood pressure monitoring

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Diazepam, a benzodiazepine, would raise the seizure threshold and reduce ECT efficacy. The correct anaesthetic agent is a short-acting one like thiopentone or propofol, not a benzodiazepine.

overallFeedback.feedback: The three modifications that define modern ECT are: short-acting general anaesthesia, succinylcholine (a muscle relaxant), and oxygenation/ventilation support. Together these prevent the musculoskeletal injuries and psychological distress of the unmodified era.

Correct! The three hallmarks of modified ECT — general anaesthesia, succinylcholine, and oxygenation — transformed this from a complication-prone procedure into one of the safest biological treatments in psychiatry.

interactions.label: A patient with severe catatonia has not responded to an adequate trial of loraze

params.question: A patient with severe catatonia has not responded to an adequate trial of lorazepam. According to the indication framework discussed, this situation justifies ECT primarily because:

answers.text: Catatonia always requires ECT as first-line treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lorazepam is actually the first-line treatment for catatonia. ECT is indicated when an adequate lorazepam trial fails, not as the initial approach.

answers.text: Failure of adequate lorazepam therapy represents medication failure — one of the three core indication scenarios for ECT

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The three indications are: urgency (patient cannot wait for medication), medication failure (as in this case), and situations where medication itself is contraindicated or hazardous.

answers.text: ECT is safer than continuing lorazepam in a catatonic patient

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The rationale is not that lorazepam is unsafe, but that it has already failed. The framework focuses on urgency, medication failure, and contraindication to pharmacotherapy.

answers.text: Catatonia is a contraindication to all pharmacological treatments

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Catatonia is not a contraindication to pharmacotherapy. Lorazepam is effective for many catatonic patients. ECT becomes indicated specifically when pharmacotherapy has failed or the situation is urgent.

overallFeedback.feedback: Lorazepam-resistant catatonia represents medication failure — one of the three core scenarios (urgency, medication failure, contraindication to pharmacotherapy) justifying ECT. This framework guards against both underuse and overuse.

Correct! The urgency–failure–contraindication framework helps clinicians decide when ECT is appropriate, preventing both underuse in real emergencies and overuse when medication has not been adequately tried.

interactions.label: Raised intracranial pressure is an absolute contraindication to electroconvulsiv

params.question: Raised intracranial pressure is an absolute contraindication to electroconvulsive therapy.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: There are no absolute contraindications to ECT. Raised intracranial pressure, recent myocardial infarction, phaeochromocytoma, and aortic aneurysm are all relative contraindications. They require extra caution and multidisciplinary involvement, but do not prohibit treatment when the indication is strong.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. There are no absolute contraindications to ECT. Raised intracranial pressure is a relative contraindication requiring extra caution and multidisciplinary input, but it does not rule out ECT when the clinical indication is compelling — such as life-threatening depression.

interactions.label: A colleague asks: 'If succinylcholine prevents the convulsion, how can ECT still

params.question: A colleague asks: 'If succinylcholine prevents the convulsion, how can ECT still work?' Which explanation correctly addresses this question?

answers.text: Succinylcholine is given at a sub-therapeutic dose that only partially blocks the seizure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Succinylcholine is given at a dose sufficient to produce full neuromuscular paralysis. The therapeutic mechanism does not depend on a partial motor convulsion persisting.

answers.text: The therapeutic effect comes from the electrical stimulus itself, not from the seizure activity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The therapeutic effect of ECT is driven by the generalised cerebral seizure, not the electrical stimulus alone. A stimulus that fails to produce a seizure on EEG is not therapeutic.

answers.text: Succinylcholine acts only at the neuromuscular junction and does not cross the blood–brain barrier, so the cerebral seizure proceeds unimpaired

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Succinylcholine blocks acetylcholine at peripheral motor end-plates but cannot cross the blood–brain barrier. The generalised cerebral seizure — the actual therapeutic mechanism — continues and is visible on EEG, while the dangerous motor convulsion is abolished.

answers.text: Modern ECT uses brief-pulse stimulation that bypasses the need for a seizure entirely

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Brief-pulse stimulation reduces cognitive side effects compared to sine-wave stimulation, but it still aims to induce a generalised seizure. The seizure remains essential for the therapeutic effect of ECT.

overallFeedback.feedback: Succinylcholine paralyses skeletal muscle by blocking the neuromuscular junction peripherally. It does not cross the blood–brain barrier, so the cerebral seizure (the actual therapeutic mechanism) proceeds unimpaired and is visible on EEG. This is key to understanding how modified ECT works.

Exactly right. This distinction — motor convulsion abolished peripherally at the neuromuscular junction, cerebral seizure preserved centrally — is the single most important concept for explaining modified ECT to patients, families, and colleagues.
